questions.question: Describe South Africa's conventional energy production — the location pattern of thermal stations, the role of hydro-electricity, and how pumped storage schemes work and why they exist.
questions.expected_answer: About 80 per cent of South Africa's electricity comes from coal burned in giant thermal stations — Kendal, Majuba, Lethabo, Matimba and the new giants Medupi and Kusile — clustered directly on the Mpumalanga, Waterberg and Free State coalfields, because sending electricity down high-voltage lines is far cheaper than railing coal across the country; Eskom's grid then carries power nationwide, with the largest flows to Gauteng. Nuclear power from Koeberg near Cape Town and small hydro make up slivers of the mix. True hydro-electricity is limited because South Africa is dry with variable rivers: stations at the Gariep and Vanderkloof dams on the Orange River help meet peaks, and imports arrive from Cahora Bassa in Mozambique. Pumped storage schemes — Drakensberg, Palmiet and Ingula — are not sources but giant batteries: two reservoirs, one high and one low; at night cheap surplus grid power pumps water uphill, and at the evening peak the water runs back through turbines. They consume more energy than they produce, but they convert cheap off-peak energy into precious peak energy and can reach full power in minutes, serving as the grid's emergency reserve.

questions.question: Explain the principles and processes of thermal electricity generation using coal, following the energy chain from coal delivery to the transmission grid, and account for the station's limited efficiency.
questions.expected_answer: The chain converts chemical energy to heat to kinetic energy to electrical energy. Coal arrives by conveyor from adjacent mines and is ground in mills to flour-fine powder, which burns fast and completely when blown into the furnace at around 1 400 degrees Celsius. The furnace walls are lined with kilometres of water-filled tubing — the boiler — where purified water becomes superheated steam beyond 500 degrees at enormous pressure. The steam jets against turbine blades, spinning the shaft at 3 000 revolutions per minute, and the shaft turns the generator, where a rotating electromagnet inside conductor coils induces electricity. Transformers step the voltage up to as much as 400 kilovolts because high voltage cuts losses over distance; substations step it down near users. Spent steam must be condensed back to water to repeat the cycle — done in hyperbolic cooling towers whose white plumes are water vapour, not smoke, or by air in dry-cooled stations like Kendal and Matimba, designed for water-scarce sites. Burning also leaves ash and flue gases carrying carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Only about a third of the coal's chemical energy leaves as electricity: a steam cycle extracts work only from the temperature difference between hot and cold, so condensing the steam necessarily rejects most of the heat to the environment — the cooling towers are the price the cycle pays to run.

questions.question: Evaluate whether South Africa can meet its long-term energy needs from conventional sources, weighing coal's advantages and disadvantages and using nuclear energy (Koeberg) as a case study.
questions.expected_answer: Coal's advantages: reserves measured in decades give energy security; shallow seams beside stations made electricity historically among the world's cheapest, founding the industrial economy; coal delivers steady baseload; the industry employs on the order of ninety thousand miners and sustains towns like Emalahleni and Secunda; and exports through Richards Bay earn foreign exchange. Its disadvantages: coal makes South Africa Africa's largest carbon dioxide emitter with carbon border taxes looming; the Highveld airshed is among the world's most polluted, with respiratory disease as the human cost; wet-cooled stations consume scarce water while acid mine drainage seeps from abandoned workings for a century; opencast mining consumes prime Mpumalanga farmland; and the ageing fleet's load-shedding proved that abundant coal fails without functioning machines, while banks no longer finance new coal. The nuclear case study: Koeberg's two reactors (about 1 900 megawatts) have supplied Western Cape baseload since 1984 through uranium fission — a fingertip pellet equalling about a tonne of coal — with no operating carbon, tiny fuel volumes and local uranium reserves; against this stand the highest construction costs and longest build times in the energy world (the new-reactor plan collapsed over affordability), radioactive waste stored at Koeberg and Vaalputs for thousands of years, and rare but enormous accident risk. Conclusion: conventional sources alone cannot carry the long term — coal is structurally constrained and nuclear is clean but slow and costly — so South Africa's realistic path is a diversified mix including renewables.
